title: transcendence of a productivity addict
content:
from my podcast, botanical studies of internet magic

listen on apple listen on spotify

I spent many years needing to feel “productive” everyday — a word that was programmed into me, and which I clung to — but which felt wholly insufficient in trying to measure creative work, especially when self-employed. in this episode, I’ll tell you my journey — from being a productivity addict — to rejecting all imposed structures — to slowly, over time, reimagining what a sustainable, nourishing system actually looks and feels like.

I made this podcast shortly after creating my zine, and in preparation for teaching a new course.

📓 Zine: Deconstructing the Productivity Machine

🪺 Creative Systems Course (live course starts Friday, March 21)

introduction

Hi friends, this is Botanical Studies of Internet Magic, a podcast on the alchemy of creative power through the vessel and portal of the internet. My name is Kening and I'll be your guide.

Today I am really excited to share with you a zine that I just finished creating last week about a topic that I've been obsessed with my entire career. I've linked a PDF to the zine in the show notes so you can download it and check it out.

Over the last 10 years I've seen how my relationship to productivity and systems has really changed from the feeling of climbing a ladder to success or enoughness every single day to thinking of systems as a web or a canopy that catches me, thinking of systems as the ground beneath my feet that if I forget what I'm doing or what day of the week it is or who I am, I can ground myself, center myself in my systems.

How This Zine Was Born

A month or so ago I had an idea to teach a course about creative systems and after I decided that I sat down to make the syllabus but I felt this urge inside of me to make a zine instead. Through this process I created the syllabus for the course using the zine format and structure to guide my thinking.


My Personal History With Productivity

Before I touch on some of the ideas I talk about in the zine I wanted to share a bit about my journey around systems. Starting up I think I can trace the origins of my obsession with productivity systems to being a child or a teenager and feeling a lot of pressure to do well academically. The need to control my limited time and energy and attention in order to fit in all of my ambitions and dreams, it was like trying to stuff a big cloud into a tiny box.

Permanently systems seemed to represent the way I was going to get from A to B, whether that was from high school to a good college or from college to a job or from a job to quitting my job, to having a business, to being an artist. It was the how, the method, it was the only way I knew I could move forward in my life.

When I went on the internet reading about how to get things done I ended up reading tons and tons of books, mostly written by men in business or tech, about getting things done literally or bullet journaling or building a second brain or time blocking. There were so many methods that I absorbed ways to manage my time, metrics, to gauge my progress and each time I would catch myself falling out of sync, feeling a lot of guilt and shame and a sense of not enoughness.


The Cycle of Systems & Burnout

Maybe the problem is that I'm not disciplined enough, I'm not focused enough, I failed at meeting my priorities for this week. I would go through this cycle of feeling exhausted and burned out from trying to keep up with whatever system to hiding and retreating and then feeling guilt and pressure and then getting a new system, thinking that if only I'm able to fit myself into this system and abide by the discipline of the system then I can get things done and reach my goals and fulfill my dreams and be safe.

In some senses this kind of works for me when I had a 9-5 job because I had a structure, I would fit in my other activities around my job. I would go to evening design classes and wake up before work to do writing and yoga. I started my first blog on the weekends. I would push myself to be disciplined, to save money, to make a plan. Feeling accomplished was really important to me because it signified that I was moving forwards I wasn't stagnant or stuck in one place.

Those routines more or less worked for me until I started working for myself and I attempted daily and weekly and monthly plans to do lists, priorities, goals. I had an entire year in which I pressured myself to the end of exhaustion with consistent output, forcing myself to follow marketing plans beyond social media and basically every day feel like I had been "productive".


Reimagining Productivity

It took me after that year of burnout to really look at the word productive and think about what it really means. The problem was that I was applying the productivity systems I've learned from school and from working a job to working for myself and it just didn't work because I found myself constantly in cycles of depletion and guilt and shame and reinventing the whole thing again and running a hamster wheel against my creative energy.

Productivity when you're working for someone else feels easy to measure because you're getting a paycheck and what you need to do is enough that your employer people around you are satisfied with your work and that you're satisfied with yourself. You're selling your labor and energy for an agreed amount of money per month. So you decide what counts as productive, what counts as having earned that money.

If you're working for yourself, if you have creative work that seems incongruent with capitalist structures and making money, how do you measure what counts as having done enough? How do you measure productivity? How do you measure the feeling of moving forward?


Creative & Material Worth

When one day of work doesn't immediately translate to a part of a paycheck, how do you decide what to spend your time on? Which activities move the wheel forwards and which don't? And I think that's a trick question because from that perspective, doing any kind of creative work doesn't move the wheel forwards to financial sustainability because you're not immediately getting paid for it.

It took me a very long time to deprogram myself from that way of thinking to prioritize the things that make money over the things that don't make money. I think the underlying theme and thread through this entire podcast and much of my work is around how creative energy and material energy is deeply connected. Creative life source feeds into the exchange of resources and doing creative work counts very much as creating resources.

But all the traditional productivity systems, even the word productivity itself made creative work or resting or anything that didn't immediately relate to generating profit feel inconsequential and unimportant.


My Pendulum Swings

For me, I can almost chart my relationship to planning and structures as a sort of pendulum swing. I started, I assume as a child, I was very free flow and playful and then pushed towards the pendulum of being very type A and planning and reading all the tech and business books, which lasted throughout college, after college, working my job, quitting my job, and then burning out the first year of trying to work for myself full time.

From there, I swung to the opposite end of the spectrum of doing the bare minimum that I could to stay alive, not planning my weeks, not planning for the future. I stopped measuring myself against the ruler of productivity. I let go of the idea of productivity and I could feel my entire body exhale a sigh of relief. This was during the pandemic. The world was in a sort of suspension mode. I created my first course that year called creative beings from this ethos of cultivating sensitivity and intuition and listening, observing, responding to the creative impulse instead of trying to control it.

I can probably identify the moment when that pendulum swang back again. It was in 2023 in which I wrote a post called a moody creatives guide to work overwhelm in which I realized I had no systems that helped me move forward and I wanted to move forward instead of existing in this free flow, creative, intuitive state.

When that shift happened, I started showing up more consistently in my work, in sharing my work, in writing newsletters. That helped. But then I found myself every week in planning mode trying to reconfigure my schedule, rearrange the pieces of my life to fit in everything that I wanted to fit in. And I would find myself stuck in these loops. And there I was swinging back and forth between imposing plans to giving up all plans and wanting to take a nap.


Transcending the Paradigm

I had escaped the productivity paradigm, but there were still parts of that thinking that were so deeply ingrained in me in which I thought to myself, if I just make a better system, if I just make new plans, then I will have solved the problem. Then I can move forward.

This year, after a much needed break and rest and integration, I found myself in a very different place in which I wouldn't say I found the balance between structure and flow or that I found a compromise between to-do lists and intuition. But instead, I feel like I've changed paradigms, like changing dimensions and transcended the pendulum swing.

I'm going to share more concretely exactly which practices have helped me a lot in this reframing. Recently, it's been working with the elements, the seasons, tarot, energy rhythms, and patterns.


Systems vs. Recipes

But today, first, let's get something clear. What is a system? The most simple definition of this is that a system contains individual parts or components that exist as discrete elements and exist together in relationship with each other. So all the parts work together as a whole, and the properties of the whole are different than the properties of each individual part.

So my creative digital system contains my website, my podcast, my newsletter, and all the creations that I share in them. These are all individual parts of my system that have a flow with each other.

So here's the thing. A system is not a recipe. In a recipe, you follow steps in a linear way, and when you're complete, you're done. The end product of the recipe is the goal. You might have linear recipes within a system, but the system as a whole is cyclical. It's simultaneous. There's a web of relationships happening at the same time, and each flows into the other. The goal of a system is for it to keep moving. For the feedback you get from the system to change the system, it's more like a growing organism.


Systems as Living Organisms

There's a regenerative living property to systems. There's things that emerge from the systems that are unexpected and spontaneous. A simple equation for a system would be inputs plus process equals output plus feedback as adaptation and emergence. Inputs are the ingredients, process is the recipe, and the output is what you get plus other unexpected surprises, and that feeds back into the input.

So in this sense, a system can be composed of recipes, but a recipe is not a system. I think the heart of this distinction gets to why I struggled so much and for many years around creative systems because I treated myself as if I was an ingredient in part of a recipe. Like if I'm focused and disciplined enough, make the time to do this thing, then I can have an output that I'm proud of.

And sometimes it happens like this. Sometimes if I set aside two hours, once a week, I can expect a consistent output. But other times it doesn't feel like this at all. Other times it feels like being inside a storm or falling down the stairs or climbing up a mountain in a delirious state. Sometimes the process feels linear and sometimes it's like a combustion. It feels so spontaneous.


Beyond the Binary of Planning vs. Flow

Part of the point I'm making is that it's not a binary between planning and not planning. It's both at the same time. But what I've found completely insufficient and even harmful in traditional productivity systems is that their impulse is to make things parceled and measurable and discrete. Whether that's time or ideas or tasks like putting all your ideas into a spreadsheet or all of your tasks into a master to-do list.

I've tried this many times. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't. It's very contingent on exactly what kind of tasks, what kind of to-do list, what kind of ideas. It's not so much the tool of organization that I am critiquing, but the mentality behind this tool which is treating your resources of time, attention, ideas, inspiration, energy as concrete blocks to manipulate, control, manage, hoard, stock, and allocate.

Even the word allocation means moving a cube of something like time up into a spot where it can grow and do its thing. But what if it doesn't? What if you allocating time or energy to a certain task backfires? I've been in that situation so many times in which I would sit down to do a task and it would feel like trudging through horse shit. And of course I always blamed myself. Why was my mind rebelling against this thing that needed to be done? Clearly it means I'm not disciplined enough.

And I thought it was a matter of willpower or focus or discipline, but over time I've realized it's because my creative energy is resistant against being allocated in that way. It wants to go where it wants to go. And I think the chaos in its movement is its power, but it's also the thing that scares us because how do we work with that which isn't always controllable? How do we build a life, a business, a system that dances with the forces of uncertainty?


Relationship with Inner Resources

And I think in that way, that's why the metaphor of nature and natural resources and natural ecosystems has resonated so much with the way that I relate to my own systems. The traditional productivity paradigm asks us to mine our limited inner resources for maximum productivity and efficiency.

But if we're to relate to our inner resources in a way that ideally we would relate to nature, it's about cultivating a symbiotic relationship with it that begins with listening and observing like a scientist or a botanist of our psyche to respect and honor its rhythms, to harness its power without depleting it to the point beyond exhaustion, and to be in a state of open receptivity to its mystery.

Moving from a framework of management to relationship ships the mindset entirely from capitalist optimization to being in reciprocal relationship. As I'm speaking, I'm reminded of a beautiful essay that I've read called The Surface Berry An Economy of Abundance by Robin Wall Kimmermer, which I will link to in the show notes.

Her way of speaking about relating to natural resources is exactly a parallel to how we can relate to our inner resources. That is, instead of trying to extract as much value per unit of time or attention as possible relating to our creative beings from a place of responsibility and sustainability. How can everything we do in our work feel regenerative? How can we be in the bounteousness of our creative resources and to share that bounteousness with others?


Integration over Compartmentalization

I think at the heart of this question is recalibrating ourselves from a mindset of compartmentalization and separation to that of integration, seeing ourselves belonging to the whole. We humans have a tendency to exploit and extract value from things that we see as wholly outside of ourselves and irrelevant to our own lives.

Traditional productivity paradigms pressures us into a mode in which we do that to ourselves, dividing our beings into the money-making self and the non-money-making self. A big part of the work is identifying all the ways in which we've disintegrated ourselves and self-sabotaged and disempowered creative energy from the whole of our material lives and well-being and begin to ask the question of what if everything was integrated?

What if I let creative energy flow through all parts of my life, all parts of my being? What if everything was connected in that how well-rested I am affects how I show up in my creative work, which affects how I do my client work? My philosophies around world-building, building websites as integrative practices translates to the way that we relate to our work on a day-to-day basis in the body, in the container of a day.


My Intentions for Systems

In closing, I want to share some intentions for the kind of systems that I want to build that I am currently building. I want, I desire deeply, systems that help me trust, systems that allow me to be absent, systems that value my rest, systems that make me more myself, systems that help me be in flow, that is meaningful exchange with myself, my creativity and the world, and systems that carry me forwards, like ships to new lands of possibility.

I also want to read you the introduction of this zine and which is also the ethos and philosophy of my course. What are systems beyond structures of imprisonment, extraction and control? Why build systems for the wilderness of the creative spirit and how do we do it without diminishing or killing its essence?

It starts with getting the machinery of productivity out of our heads, deprogramming as liberation, then slowly cultivating a new relationship with our inner and life resources, time, attention, energy, inspiration. Not as limited reserves to mine or hoard or control, but as fluid entities like the weather or the ebb and flow of tidal waves or the moon.

Therefore, the systems we build for human cosmic natural bodies must be born from deep observation, inquiry, listening, surrender, response. We ask it what it needs to feel held and safe, to rest and dream, to reimagine and expand. We reinvent our systems like writing our own languages, trusting them to speak for us, making new worlds of care and regeneration.


Closing

Thank you, creative friends, for being here and for listening. You can download the creative system zine in the show notes and if you're interested in the course, I'm teaching a live run Friday, March 21st until April 11th. It will be two hour video sessions and guided experiments.

My intention for this course is not to teach you any new systems, but to help you tune into your natural rhythms and slowly piece together your own systems that are molded and shaped to your creative body.

Currently, I also teach a self-paced course called House on the Webs and offer one-on-one advising sessions as well as creation services through my web alchemy studio, Other Worldly. You can find more of my work and writings on my website, Keningzhu.com. I currently send twice monthly newsletters, which you can sign up for in the show notes.

I'll look forward to speaking to you again soon.
